style_reason: Light, colour and air are invisible; cut-paper layers make a physical, touchable world where a white paper beam can literally split into coloured ribbons and scatter into blue paper flecks. The rooftop gives a familiar Indian everyday setting to open and close on.

story.idea: A child on a sunny rooftop looks up: the sky is blue, yet sunlight looks white. Why?
White sunlight hides all the rainbow colours; a prism reveals them.
Tiny air molecules scatter light every way; short blue waves scatter far more than long red ones.
Scattered blue reaches the eye from the whole sky, so every direction looks blue (back on the rooftop).
Violet scatters even more, but sunlight has less violet and eyes favour blue.
At sunset light crosses a long path; blue is scattered away and red-orange arrives: the same rooftop turns orange.

guardrails: no wavelength numbers, percentages or the 1/lambda^4 law (not stated by the sources read)
do not name nitrogen or oxygen
molecules are symbolic dots, never drawn to scale
the violet strip and eye-sensitivity visual are illustrative only, without values
do not suggest red light is never scattered; it is scattered much less
sunset colours are illustrative; do not suggest pollution causes the sunset
